title: Five (Uncomfortable) Questions That Made Me a Better Consultant
author: Andrea Chiarelli
summary: Chiarelli argues that the hardest moments in consulting are not technical but are pointed questions that test a leader's credibility, integrity and accountability. She walks through five client questions: can you do it faster, can you make the report say what we want, why should we listen to you, can you just add this in, and can you fix this. For each she gives the response that worked for her and the takeaway behind it. The move is to treat each uncomfortable question as a mirror of the professional you want to be, and to answer with calm, honesty and ownership rather than appeasement or blame. Her reflections close by tying these moments to reputation, since saying no with clarity and empathy builds trust.
points: Respond to pressure to speed up by naming the trade-off, what would be cut and what the client would lose, so the choice is informed rather than reflexive.
Integrity is not stubborn purity; it means holding the line where it matters most and communicating it with diplomacy.
An outsider reframes weakness as strength by positioning herself as the one who brings structure and spots patterns insiders overlook.
Absorbing scope creep silently sets a precedent; framing extra work as a new piece of work turns a no into a professional boundary.
Accountability flows upward: the lead owns the error, takes the blame, and redirects energy to a fix, which is what earns long-term trust.
quotes: The problem here is not just working late hours (which I don’t encourage you do!) - it’s that real insight takes iteration, testing and buy-in from stakeholders. Cut that short, and the plan will look neat on paper but fall flat in practice.

The hard part in these cases is holding your ground without sounding inflexible. My usual go-to is to frame it in terms of risk: “Yes, we can go faster, but here’s what we would have to cut. And here’s what you would lose.

In those moments, you can’t compete on years of experience. What you can do is reframe your role: “You’re the experts on the industry. My role is to bring structure, to spot patterns and to ask the questions that insiders sometimes overlook because they are too close to the matter.” This kind of shift turns the challenge into a strength.
Early in my career, I tried to absorb all of these requests quietly, thinking it showed flexibility. It didn’t. It set a precedent that anything could be added without consequence.
Blame is tempting (especially if you suspect you know what the source was), but it destroys trust. By accepting responsibility, you shift the focus from finger-pointing to problem-solving.
The hardest questions were about credibility, integrity and accountability. Each one cut to the heart of what it means to be trusted in a role where you have influence but not control.
